html: One more distinction is worth keeping. Every robot is a kind of automation, but not every piece of automation is a robot. A fixed conveyor belt or a machine built for a single job is automated. But it is not reprogrammable or multipurpose, and those are the words ISO uses to mark the line.

SAE assigns a level to the driving feature that is switched on at a given moment, not to the car as a whole. It also leaves out momentary interventions such as automatic emergency braking.[16] That is a useful habit for robots too: ask how autonomous a machine is while doing a particular task.

Drone: the IEEE guide lists drones among robots that “take to the skies.”[13] Under ISO, a drone flown entirely by a pilot looks more like a robotic device. One that holds its position or flies a route by itself has the autonomy to be a mobile robot.

In 1961 the first Unimate went to work at General Motors, at GM’s plant in Ewing Township near Trenton, New Jersey. The plant was then run by the Ternstedt division of GM’s Fisher Body unit (it was later called Inland Fisher Guide), which is why sources call it the Ternstedt plant.[17][23][24] The job was handling hot die-cast parts. The arm, about 4,000 lb (1,800 kg), lifted die-cast pieces of up to about 40 lb and dropped them into cooling pools. It was a hot and dangerous job that three shifts of workers had done before.[23] After roughly 100,000 hours of work the robot was donated to the Smithsonian in 1971, and the Unimate joined the Robot Hall of Fame in 2003.[23][20]

Collaborative robots, or cobots, are designed to work alongside people in shared spaces. Their speed and force limits are configured as part of their setup. Many can be taught by lead-through, a form of hand guiding: the operator physically guides the arm through the waypoints of a task.[14] Universal Robots’ e-Series, programmed through PolyScope 5, is a common example.[15]

OSHA also says that anyone who programs, operates or maintains a robot should receive adequate safety training before being assigned. It adds that removing or engineering away a hazard is preferred over relying on rules and protective equipment.[2] The main international standard is ISO 10218, revised in 2025. The new edition makes functional safety requirements more explicit, absorbs the cobot guidance from ISO/TS 15066, and adds cybersecurity requirements as they relate to safety.[3] Its collaborative modes were introduced in 1.3 Types of Robots.

Robots that work around people need predictable behavior. A hospitality robot in a hotel is often organized as a state machine (a model where a robot switches between distinct operational states based on inputs). Example states are Idle (waiting for a wake word), Listening and Responding. A rule on top makes the robot slow or stop whenever a person comes too close.

A cell goes one step further. It is the robot system plus everything an integrator adds so that it can do one job safely and repeatably. That ranges from part feeding and sensors to a coordinating controller and guarding.

The robot is rarely the slow part here. Cycle time in machine tending is driven by machining time, the door and chuck sequence, and reliable part presentation, not by the robot's top speed.[31] On an older machine, the robot can open and close the CNC door itself, so the cell does not need an automatic door driven by a signal. Robotiq reports this works well in many integrations, while for a new machine an automatic door is generally worth its cost.[32]

A palletizing cell stacks cases onto pallets at the end of a packaging line. Pearson's RPC cell is a typical example: an empty pallet is dispensed onto a three-strand drag chain conveyor and carried to the loading position. The robot places slip sheets (protective separator sheets that keep the stacked load stable) between layers when needed. Pearson rates it at 20 cases per minute steady state, with surges to 30.[33] Arpac's LT palletizer uses a “smart” infeed conveyor that separates the products, has a fully interlocked operator door and a light curtain, and is rated at up to 15 cases per minute.[34] Grippers are often vacuum plates.[35] The Arpac LT, for example, uses a dual-zone vacuum plate gripper that handles one or two cases at a time, and a light curtain guards the opening where full pallets leave the cell.[36] These are vendor ratings, not guarantees.

Offline programming (OLP) generates robot programs on a computer instead of on the physical robot, which only stops while the new program is downloaded and tested.[3][6] The programmer works inside a 3D simulation built from CAD models of the robot, tooling, parts, and fixtures. FANUC ROBOGUIDE, for example, imports CAD models to build accurate layouts and uses virtual robots to design and visualize cells.[17]

Second, teaching is done at reduced speed. OSHA guidance states that robot speeds during programming sessions are below 250 mm/s (10 inches per second).[5] ABB's manual states that in manual reduced speed mode the movement is limited to 250 mm/s.[7] This ceiling gives an operator close to the arm time to release the enabling device or press the emergency stop before a collision.

Programming an industrial robot requires tools that connect high-level task logic with real-time mechanical motion. General software developers write source code in text editors, compile it, and test it on a computer. In robotics, the software must also coordinate physical arms, grippers, safety interlocks, and programmable logic controllers (PLCs). In a modern robotic cell the PLCs and robot controllers must be integrated with each other.[1]

Part of the reason is timing. A robot controller is not a desktop computer running ordinary programs whenever it gets around to them. It runs a real-time motion system that must send fresh commands to the arm on a fixed, very short cycle. Universal Robots' e-Series manual, for example, states that the robot must be controlled at 500 Hz, which means the controller has to tell the arm what to do every 0.002 seconds. It also states that URScript programs are executed in real time in the controller's RuntimeMachine.[2] A vendor language lets the manufacturer run user programs inside that tightly controlled loop.

Universal Robots' script language, URScript, looks friendlier than RAPID.[2] Functions are defined with def and closed with end, the lines inside a block must be indented, and variables do not need type declarations. The manual states that a variable's type is deduced from its first assignment. If you know Python, the syntax will feel familiar.

A central master (roscore): In ROS 1, nodes connect to each other directly, but they find each other through a name service called the master (started by roscore). Connection set-up is negotiated over XML-RPC.[1] Every node therefore depends on that one master. The ROS 2 design team noted that multi-robot systems had no standard approach and were “somewhat of a hack on top of the single-master structure of ROS.”[11]

Navigation 2 (Nav2): Nav2 is the professionally supported successor of the original ROS Navigation Stack.[6] It uses a behavior tree to coordinate its navigation tasks,[16] and its task servers load plugins for planners, controllers, and behaviors. The documentation covers planners such as NavFn and Smac and controllers such as DWB, MPPI, and Regulated Pure Pursuit.[6] Nav2 builds a model of the environment from sensor data and plans around obstacles in it.[6] Its developers tested it by having a robot navigate safely alongside students on a university campus over a marathon-length distance.[16]

ros2_control hardware interface: The hardware interface is implemented with the ros2_control framework. It does not decide how the robot moves by itself; standard controllers such as the JointTrajectoryController (used with MoveIt 2) or a force-mode controller do that. The interface also exposes force-torque sensor data, speed scaling, and I/O.[20][18]

Dashboard client: A dashboard client talks to the robot's dashboard server and exposes ROS 2 services such as power_on, brake_release, load_program, play, and unlock_protective_stop. With these, a ROS program can start the robot and clear a protective stop (after its cause is fixed) without using the teach pendant.[20]

The vacuum itself comes either from an electric pump or from an ejector (a venturi device that creates vacuum from a flow of compressed air). Piab, an ejector maker, says ejectors generate no heat or vibration and reduce noise, while conceding that they consume a lot of compressed air.[5] How the ejector is built matters for that air bill. In a stamping study at DaimlerChrysler, multistage ejectors used 1.1 SCFM (standard cubic feet per minute, a measure of how much compressed air flows) per cycle, up to 78% less than single-stage generators. An air-saving check valve that shuts off the air once vacuum is reached reduced consumption further.[6] Piab also claims up to 50% lower compressed-air cost for its compact P2010 multistage ejector, which runs from a 26 psi feed.[7] Treat these as vendor figures: no independent comparison of ejectors and pumps was found for this lesson.

Electric grippers also differ in how they talk to the controller. Zimmer's GEP2000 series comes in three sizes, with 10, 13 and 16 mm of stroke per jaw and up to 200, 360 and 500 N of grip force. Each size is offered with plain digital I/O, with a 0-10 V position-feedback signal, or with IO-Link (a standard digital link that connects one sensor or actuator to an industrial controller).[9] A GEP2000-B variant adds detection of a lost workpiece that is reported to the controller.[10] Vention sells a Universal Robots package for the 16 mm Zimmer gripper (125 to 500 N, 24 V, 2 A maximum, 0.02 mm repeatability) aimed at sites with no compressed air.[11] The choice of interface decides what your program can know: a digital-only gripper reports at most "open" or "closed", while an analog or IO-Link version can report where the jaws actually stopped.

A popup is not a safety function. Users on UR's forum point out that a popup followed by halt cannot be resumed, and a popup without halt does not stop the program at all. For real safety behavior they are directed to the configured safety functions, such as a protective stop, rather than script messages.[26] UR does document a protective_stop() script function, and UR's error code C209 reads "A protective stop was triggered (for test purposes only)".[27][28] Error handling keeps production running and tells people what went wrong; it does not protect people. Guarding, safety-rated stops and safety I/O do that, as covered in 5.4 Making a Robot Cell Safe.

Apply that to a typical cell. A camera 1280 pixels wide viewing a 320 mm field gives 4 pixels per millimetre, or 0.25 mm per pixel. With the 2 to 4 pixel rule, the smallest feature it can locate reliably is about 0.5 to 1 mm. Halve the FOV to 160 mm and each pixel covers half as much. That is why a wrist camera that moves closer can see finer detail than a fixed camera that must see the whole table.

Splitting a robot into small nodes also helps when things go wrong. Because nodes can run as separate processes,[9] a crash in the camera driver (for example, after a USB glitch) does not have to take down the motor controller or a safety monitor running in other processes. The driver can be restarted on its own without rebooting the robot.

A topic gives no built-in acknowledgment that the job is done. A service is the wrong tool too. The documentation says services are expected to return quickly because the client is generally waiting. They should never be used for long-running processes that might need to be preempted, for example if a person walks in front of the robot.[15]

ROS 2's default middleware is DDS, and nodes find each other automatically through that middleware. A new node advertises itself to other nodes in the same ROS domain, and they reply with information about themselves.[25][26] DDS discovery uses multicast, so the network interface must have multicast enabled.[27]
Why is it safer for an industrial robot to split the work into separate nodes that do not wait for each other, rather than run all motor drivers and computer vision logic inside one big loop?

That transition period is now over. ROS Noetic Ninjemys, the last ROS 1 distribution, was marked End-of-Life (EOL) on May 31, 2025. After the final sync on May 29, no new Noetic changes were accepted and regressions in binary packages could no longer be fixed.[25][26] ROS 1 has reached the end of development with no new releases planned, while ROS 2 releases a new distribution every year.[26]

The second argument to declare_parameter is the default value, which also fixes the parameter's type. Changing a declared parameter's type at runtime fails unless it was declared with dynamic typing allowed.[13][3] If a node you write in lesson 4.6 should read a value from a YAML file, it must declare that parameter first.

Universal Robots maintains its own ROS 2 driver, built on the Universal_Robots_Client_Library. It works with all UR robots from 3 kg to 30 kg payload on PolyScope X, PolyScope 5 and CB3 controllers. It supports pausing at an emergency stop or safeguard stop, "automatic speed scaling to avoid violate the safety setting" and manual speed scaling from the teach pendant.[18] Its release table lists Humble, Jazzy, Kilted, Lyrical and Rolling, and the README states that "a fundamental requirement for the driver is using Linux".[18] It is one of the few drivers already released for ROS 2 Lyrical: the Lyrical distribution file lists ur_robot_driver version 6.2.0-1 with its calibration, controller, dashboard, MoveIt configuration and driver packages.[7]

MotoROS2 offers a follow_joint_trajectory action, so it fits the common pattern, but it is a trajectory-forwarding driver with clear limits. Before sending a goal, a client must check robot_status, make the trajectory start at the robot's current state ("MotoROS2 will reject any trajectory which does not start at the current state") and call start_traj_mode. A trajectory may hold at most 200 points, state publishing is capped at about 100 Hz. There is no Cartesian motion, no asynchronous multi-group motion and not yet any replacing of a trajectory while it runs.[11]

A key idea in the 2025 revision is that collaboration belongs to the application, not to the robot alone. The terms "collaborative robot" and "collaborative operation" no longer appear in ISO 10218; the standard speaks of "collaborative applications" instead.[8][7] The revision also folded in the collaborative-application content of ISO/TS 15066, made functional safety requirements more explicit, and added cybersecurity requirements that relate to robot safety.[8][7] In practice, a robot arm with rounded edges and torque sensing can still be part of a dangerous application if it carries a sharp sheet of laser-cut steel or a cutting torch. So the whole application (robot, end-effector, workpiece and surroundings) must be risk-assessed.

To make power and force limiting measurable, ISO/TS 15066 gives a table of biomechanical limits. They come from a pain-onset study (project FP-0317) at the University of Mainz with 100 healthy adult volunteers, and they cover 29 specific body areas grouped into body regions.[10][11] For each body region the specification gives a maximum permissible force for quasi-static contact (clamping or crushing where a body part can be trapped). Separate pressure limits (in N/cm²) are given for the specific body areas.[12][10]

Autonomous mobile machinery: An autonomous machine may have a supervisor. The machine must send information and alerts to the supervisor, who must be able to stop it, restart it, or move it to a safe position. The machine must also operate safely within a defined working area.[16]

During final commissioning, the lead safety engineer finds an intermittent fault. When an autonomous pallet jack enters the collaborative zone, the laser area scanner sometimes fails to switch the robot into reduced speed. The cause is sunlight glinting off the polished concrete floor.

In ordinary software, an unhandled exception or a deadlock crashes a process or corrupts a record. In robotics, a software bug or a bypassed interlock can let a heavy steel arm move while a person is within reach. OSHA's accident cases show workers struck, or crushed against posts and fixtures, in exactly this way.[1] Physical safety is therefore not just a compliance checkbox: it is the first ethical obligation an engineer owes to the people who share space with a machine.

For machinery, the main functional safety standard is ISO 13849-1:2023, which gives a method for designing the safety-related parts of control systems, including their software.[10] It rates each safety function with a Performance Level from PL a (lowest) to PL e (highest), defined by its probability of a dangerous failure per hour. For PL e this is between 10−8 and 10−7 per hour.[11] The PL achieved depends on the architecture category (B, 1, 2, 3 or 4), the reliability of the parts, the diagnostic coverage and protection against common-cause failures.[12] Robot safety controllers are commonly certified to PL d, Category 3, as the ABB and Universal Robots examples below show.[13][14]

In a landmark 2018 study, Joy Buolamwini and Timnit Gebru tested commercial gender-classification systems and found that darker-skinned women were the most misclassified group, with error rates of up to 34.7%. The maximum error rate for lighter-skinned men was 0.8%.[20] Similar problems matter for robots and vehicles that must detect people in order to avoid them:

Source: IFR, World Robotics 2024.[5] China's density rose from 402 in 2022 to 470 in 2023, overtaking Germany and Japan, and the IFR attributes this to the country's push to use automation technology.[5] Density figures show where robots are used most, but on their own they do not tell us what robots do to jobs and wages. That question needs studies such as Acemoglu and Restrepo's, which compare places with different exposure over time.[2]

The severity of these risks was highlighted in December 2022, when MIT Technology Review reported that development versions of iRobot's Roomba J7 series had taken intimate photographs inside homes in 2020, including one of a woman on the toilet.[9] The images were sent to Scale AI, whose contract workers in Venezuela labeled them to train the robot's AI. Some of those workers posted them in private groups on Facebook, Discord and other platforms.[9] iRobot said the images came from special development robots given to paid data collectors and employees who had signed written agreements acknowledging that video and other data would be sent back for training.[9]

Elish developed the idea from high-profile accidents involving complex automated socio-technical systems. Her sources include the Three Mile Island nuclear accident, the loss of Air France flight 447 and the 2018 crash of an Uber self-driving test vehicle in Tempe, Arizona.[12] In such cases the human operator tends to be blamed for failing to intervene in time, even though people are poorly suited to monitoring an automated system passively for long periods and then taking over at a moment's notice.

Several frameworks can structure this thinking. IEEE 7000-2021 gives a process for eliciting stakeholders' values and tracing them into system requirements.[14] The EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) regulates AI by risk. It prohibits some AI practices outright, sets requirements for high-risk systems (risk management, technical documentation and record-keeping, and human oversight) and adds transparency obligations for certain other AI systems.[15] In 2026, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 moved AI in machinery, such as industrial robots, under the EU Machinery Regulation (Annex I, Section B of the AI Act), which is to add the AI requirements through delegated acts by 2 August 2028.[16] Before deploying an autonomous robot into a shared workspace, a public space or a home, ask five questions:

Draft a design proposal for an autonomous drone delivery system that removes the "moral crumple zone". Define clear handoffs between the autonomous flight software and the remote human dispatchers, and say what is logged at each handoff.

Fences. The height of a fence and its distance from the hazard are set by ISO 13857, whose current edition (2019) was reconfirmed in 2025. It covers people aged 14 and older; the 5th-percentile stature of a 14-year-old is about 1400 mm.[11] The fence maker Troax advises that protective structures lower than 1400 mm should not be used without additional safety measures. It adds that reach-over distances come from ISO 13857 Table 2, which relates the hazard height, the fence height and the horizontal distance between them.[12] Openings in the fence must be sized under the same standard, so that fingers, arms or a whole body cannot reach through.

For coarser curtains (resolutions from 40 to 70 mm), Datalogic gives K = 1600 mm/s and a reach-over allowance of C = 850 mm, with the highest beam at 900 mm and the lowest beam at 300 mm.[18] ReeR gives the same K and C for resolutions of 50 to 90 mm.[19] These rules and examples follow the long-used 2010 edition of ISO 13855, as presented in vendor guides. The current edition, ISO 13855:2024, which replaced the 2010 edition, restates the formula as S = (K × T) + DDS + Z, where DDS takes the place of C and Z is an application-dependent supplement. It also adds new cases such as mobile applications. Check the current text before you position a real safeguard.[20][21]

Teach mode is a special case, because a programmer must stand near a powered robot to jog it and record points. Two measures protect them. The first is reduced speed. In the Universal Robots manual, the speed of the tool center point and of the elbow both start limited to 250 mm/s in teach or program mode. The speed slider can raise the limit, but activating the enabling device resets it to 250 mm/s.[26] The second is a three-position enabling device on the pendant. On UR15, UR20 and UR30 robots, manual-mode motion requires holding the enabling button in its center position. Releasing it, or squeezing it fully in a panic grip, stops the robot immediately; UR classes this as a category 2 stop. UR says this three-position-enabling pendant is mandatory for those models under ISO 10218-1:2025.[27] The UR manual also recommends pairing the enabling device with a mode switch wired as a safety input.[26]

At NVIDIA's GTC conference in March 2025, UR's parent company Teradyne and its partners showed version 1.1 of the AI Accelerator, which integrates NVIDIA Isaac Manipulator components. In one partner demo (from Groundlight), the system "trains a model to detect a workpiece and generate a robot program for picking."[2] At GTC Paris in June 2025, a UR15 arm running PolyScope X picked objects whose positions it was not given in advance, to show how applications built with the AI Accelerator cope with variation. UR reportedly named machine tending and bin picking as target uses.[3]

Frames. A pose only means something relative to a frame: the robot base, the tool, or a feature frame on the fixture. URScript's pose_add adds an offset in the base frame, while pose_trans applies an offset expressed in the frame of the first pose. So pose_trans(pick, p[0, 0, -0.05, 0, 0, 0]) means "50 mm back along the tool's own Z axis." Mixing them up is a classic error. When the tool points straight down, its Z axis points the opposite way to the base's Z axis, so an offset meant to back the tool away from a part can instead drive it 50 mm into the part. A wrong tool center point (TCP) setting causes the same kind of silent offset.

In this capstone you build a complete robot work cell in software. A simulated arm picks a part from an infeed position, places it at an outfeed position, uses simulated I/O for its gripper and a part-present sensor, and respects a safety configuration you set up yourself. It must also pass a test sheet modelled on a factory acceptance test (FAT: a formal check at the supplier's facility that the equipment meets the contract specifications before delivery). You can use either Universal Robots' URSim or ABB RobotStudio. Both are free to start, and both run the same controller software a real robot runs.

Keep the limits of simulation in mind when you write up T04 to T06. A cell can pass a demonstration in the shop and still fail on site, because parameters, networks and interfaces differ there. Integrators therefore treat the robot, controls, safety functions and plant interfaces as one system with documented acceptance criteria.[23] Your test sheet is a first version of those criteria, not a substitute for a real FAT and site acceptance test.

Detecting a stall or a lost encoder. Both look the same from the controller's point of view: the commanded PWM is high but the measured speed is about zero. Start a timer when that condition becomes true and clear it when it stops being true. If it stays true longer than a limit you choose (a few hundred milliseconds is a reasonable starting point), go to FAULT. Choose the PWM threshold from your open-loop table: it should be clearly above the dead zone. Given the stall current, this check is what protects the driver, so test it in M3.

It is a monitor, not a controller. It reads and reports, and it never clears a stop on its own. UR's service manual says robot stops must never be acknowledged and reset automatically; resuming must be a deliberate action by a person.[1] Safety functions stay on the safety-rated paths from 5.4 Making a Robot Cell Safe and 8.4 Safety over the Network.

High-level robotic architectures such as ROS 2 often run on single-board computers or PCs with a general-purpose operating system like Linux. A standard Linux kernel is not set up as a real-time operating system. The mainline kernel offers several preemption models, and only the "Fully Preemptible Kernel" model turns Linux into a real-time OS. Without it, a time-critical thread can be held up by other work, so its timing is not guaranteed.[1]

Each GPIO pin can supply only a small current, and the limit differs between boards. On the Uno R3, Arduino lists 20 mA per I/O pin, and the ATmega328P's absolute maximum rating is 40 mA per pin. The 20 mA figure is the datasheet's test condition at 5 V, not a safe target to run at continuously.[3][7] On the Uno R4, Arduino states that the RA4M1's GPIOs can handle up to 8 mA and warns never to connect devices that draw more current directly to a GPIO.[5]

Incremental Encoders: An incremental encoder produces a stream of pulses as the shaft turns, so it can only report a change in position. The controller counts pulses relative to wherever it started.[1][3] It keeps no record of its position, so when the power goes off, its position is forgotten and the robot has to home again. After power-up, the system must move to an index or home position to recover its location.[1] Some incremental encoders provide a third index channel (Channel Z) for this, which pulses once per revolution;[4] a counter can reload a known value when the index signal appears.[5]

If a program tries to catch these transitions by polling the encoder pins with digitalRead() inside loop(), it must check the pins constantly to avoid missing pulses, which leaves almost no time for anything else. Any slow step in the loop means missed counts and a position error that builds up.[11]

As an illustration, picture an industrial robot cell where an arm holds a heavy welding fixture inside a car body. With incremental encoders, an emergency stop or power outage would lose the joint positions. To re-home, the arm would have to move each joint until it found its home switch, possibly colliding with the car body and tooling on the way. With absolute encoders, the controller reads every joint angle as soon as power returns, with no movement, so production can resume safely.[1]

Electromagnetic Interference (EMI): Encoder signals are fast, low-voltage digital pulses. Running encoder wires alongside motor cables that carry PWM current can couple noise into them and cause false counts. Route encoder wiring away from motor power cables, and use twisted-pair or shielded cable where noise is a problem. Industrial interfaces such as SSI use twisted pairs for this reason.[6] Industrial encoders reduce noise further with differential (RS-422 line-driver) outputs, which send each channel together with its inverse so that noise picked up equally on both wires cancels at the receiver.[18]

Rather than commanding raw actuator power, roboticists command a target setpoint (such as maintaining a velocity of 0.50 m/s or rotating an elbow joint to exactly 45.0 degrees). To reach and hold this target despite changing loads and disturbances, the robot must measure its actual state with feedback sensors (such as quadrature encoders), compute the tracking error and adjust its actuator commands automatically. The most widely used algorithm for this job is the Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) controller. Åström and Murray state that more than 95% of all industrial control problems are solved by PID control, many of them with the derivative term left out (PI control).[2]

Infrared Reflectance Arrays (Pololu QTR-8RC): Pair an infrared emitter LED with an infrared phototransistor pointed directly downward toward the floor.[16] White surfaces reflect much more infrared light back to the phototransistor than dark matte tape, so the reading tells the robot whether it is over the line. The QTR-8RC places eight emitter and phototransistor pairs at a 9.525 mm (0.375 in) pitch. Pololu gives an optimal sensing distance of 3 mm (0.125 in) and a maximum recommended sensing distance of 9.5 mm (0.375 in). Mounted higher than that, the contrast between line and floor becomes unreliable.[16]

To bring formal structure to robot behavior, engineers use a Finite State Machine (FSM).[2] An FSM is a mathematical model of computation made of a fixed set of states, incoming events and guarded transitions between states. At any instant, the robot is in exactly one state. State machines separate what the robot does (the state action) from when it switches behaviors (the state transition). This organizes the "think" stage of the sense-think-act cycle into modular software components that are easier to check.

Action: Executable code invoked by the state machine. In classic automata theory, state machines execute actions either during states (a Moore machine) or during state transitions (a Mealy machine). Harel's statecharts allow both, and also allow actions on entering and on leaving a state.[2] In embedded robot code it is common to split a state's work into entry actions (run once on arrival, such as resetting a timer), execution actions (run on every pass of the control loop), and exit actions (run once on leaving, such as turning off an indicator LED).

This section is the lesson's own worked example. To see an FSM in action, take a differential-drive robot with two analog floor reflectance sensors (A0 and A1), an HC-SR04 ultrasonic range finder (trigger pin 9, echo pin 10; the module measures roughly 2 cm to 4 m),[3] two DC motors controlled via PWM H-bridge drivers, and a normally high digital emergency stop push-button (pin 2).

Transitions: Boolean conditions between steps. A transition is enabled when all of its preceding steps are active, and it "clears" when it is enabled and its condition is true. Clearing hands activity from the preceding steps to the following ones.[11]

The package documentation describes how to split estimation between two filter instances. An instance that fuses only continuous data (wheel odometry, visual odometry, IMU) uses the odom frame as its world frame. An instance that also fuses global absolute data such as GPS uses the map frame, and something else (normally the first instance) must provide the odom → base_link transform. Both nodes publish their estimate on odometry/filtered by default.[8] The package's GPS guide explains the reason: GPS data is subject to discrete jumps, which makes a position estimate that includes it unfit for navigation modules. So it recommends one instance that fuses only continuous data such as odometry and IMU in the odom frame and a second instance that fuses all sources, including GPS, in the map frame.[15] These frames follow ROS REP 105, in which the pose in the odom frame is continuous but can drift without bound, while the map frame is not continuous and can change in discrete jumps.[16] This dual-EKF arrangement separates smooth motor control from absolute global positioning:

WPILib handles this case explicitly. After computing the cruise distance, the code checks whether it is negative, with the comment "Handle the case where the profile never reaches full speed". If it is, the code sets the acceleration time to sqrt(dist / maxAcceleration) and the cruise distance to zero, which is the triangle above.[4] Corke's toolbox approaches the same limit from a different direction. Its trapezoidal() function takes the move duration as given and checks the requested speed V. It raises "V too small" if the speed could not cover the distance in time, and "V too big" if V is more than twice the average speed, which is the point where the trapezoid has collapsed into a triangle.[5]

Near a kinematic singularity—a configuration where joint axes align and eliminate one or more degrees of freedom—that step becomes a problem. A classic case on a six-axis arm is the wrist singularity, where joint 5 is close to zero and two wrist axes line up. Holding a constant TCP speed through that region can demand very large joint speeds, so the controller slows, stops or reports an error. ABB's RAPID manual offers SingArea \Wrist, which lets the tool orientation differ somewhat so a linear move can pass the wrist singularity, where axes 4 and 6 are parallel (axis 5 at 0 degrees). The setting applies until the next SingArea instruction, and SingArea \Off is the default.[13][24] Users on ABB's forum add a second way through: replace the move with a MoveJ.[25] One forum thread reports that ABB support confirmed MoveL errors cannot be caught with an error handler, and suggests checking the path first with non-motion execution, which runs the program without moving the robot.[26]

In robotic work cell integration, two physical dimensions determine the required lens focal length: field of view (FOV) and working distance (WD). The field of view is the area being inspected, which must fill the camera sensor. Working distance is the clearance between the front of the lens and the inspected object. For example, for a given sensor format, increasing the working distance enlarges the field of view. Shortening the focal length gives a broad field of view within a compact space.

In 7.1 Industrial Cameras and Optics, we studied camera sensors, pixel pitch, shutter mechanisms, and lenses. In 2.8 Vision-Guided Picking, we examined how robots use vision data to compute physical grasping offsets. When a robot cell has contrast or measurement errors, a common beginner mistake is to assume that the camera resolution is too low or that the image processing must be made more complex. In the factory, machine vision begins with illumination.

A machine vision camera cannot inspect features it cannot see. Desired image quality can typically be achieved by improving system illumination rather than investing in higher resolution detectors or lenses.[1] For example, an expensive high-resolution camera paired with a precision lens will still produce unusable results if improper lighting creates harsh glare or deep shadows. In contrast, an inexpensive sensor under well-arranged lighting gives clean, consistent images that simple, fast algorithms can process reliably.

Some jobs inspect features on the front face of an opaque object, such as reading character codes, verifying component placement, or inspecting surface finish. For these, light must be directed from the front. The angle at which light strikes the surface determines how textures, edges, and flaws appear.

However, sensor pixel count alone does not guarantee that fine edges or small defects can be resolved clearly. As 7.1 explained, optical resolution is measured in line pairs per millimeter and the Nyquist limit is two pixels per line pair,[3] and the lens must also keep enough contrast between the bars.[4] For gauging, this means that if a detail on the object is smaller than two sensor pixels, the vision system cannot reliably detect it or find where its edge is.

Every image message begins with a standard ROS header structure containing timing and coordinate frame metadata. In sensor_msgs/Image the header timestamp represents image acquisition time and frame_id specifies the optical frame of the camera.[2] A driver should stamp each image with the time it was captured. That timestamp is needed to match vision data with joint encoder states when a robot arm moves while its eye-in-hand camera takes images, or when tracking moving conveyor belts.

For example, suppose a vision node requires synchronized access to both image data and calibration parameters. In Python, the node constructs two message_filters.Subscriber objects, passing the node, the message type and the topic name. It then creates a TimeSynchronizer filter that takes both filter sources and a queue size (such as 10 frames). The node registers a dual-argument callback sync_callback(image_msg, info_msg) using registerCallback. Whenever an image message and a calibration message share identical header timestamps, the synchronizer invokes the callback with both messages matched together. If one message arrives late, the synchronizer holds the other in its queue until the match arrives or the queue overflows, so the callback never sees an image paired with the wrong calibration.

Every MQTT application message has a Topic Name and a Quality of Service.[4] Clients publish messages to the server (often called a broker) under a topic name such as plant/cell_2/robot_1/temperature, and the server forwards them to the clients that subscribed to that topic. Publishers and subscribers never connect to each other directly.

For example, an automated guided vehicle (AGV) transporting parts between cells publishes its battery voltage to topic agv_3/battery every ten seconds with QoS 0. It publishes batch completion notices to topic agv_3/completed on port 8883 with QoS 2, so that the inventory database records the delivery without duplicates.
